_note: Bordeaux classified estates for the Deep Region (pipeline/bordeaux_deep.py). Names follow French and English Wikipedia, iDealwine and the INAO / AGCCSE list for Saint-Émilion 2022; the official sites of the Conseil des Grands Crus Classés en 1855 could not be read when this list was made. Locations: the château's coordinates on Wikipedia, else its OpenStreetMap point. Estates without a checked location are listed on their appellation but not drawn.

medoc_1855.title: Classification of 1855, Médoc (red)
medoc_1855.note: The list was drawn up by Bordeaux brokers for the Paris Universal Exhibition of 1855 and ranked estates by price. It covers 60 Médoc estates plus Haut-Brion in the Graves. Apart from Mouton in 1973 and the addition of Cantemerle it has never been revised.

estates.name: Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande

medoc_1855.revisions: Cantemerle added as a Cinquième Cru shortly after the original list (handwritten addition dated 16 September 1855 per French sources; usually given as 1856). Mouton Rothschild promoted from Deuxième to Premier Cru in 1973. Third growth Dubignon disappeared (absorbed by Malescot St. Exupéry and Château Margaux around 1960). Several estates split later: Léoville (3), Pichon (2), Boyd (Boyd-Cantenac, Cantenac Brown), Batailley (Haut-Batailley); Pouget-Lassale merged into Pouget.

sauternes_1855.title: Classification of 1855, Sauternes and Barsac (sweet white)
sauternes_1855.note: Made at the same time as the Médoc list for the 1855 exhibition. Château d'Yquem alone holds Premier Cru Supérieur. Barsac estates may label as Barsac or Sauternes.
sauternes_1855.revisions: No change in rank. The original 21 entries became 27 estates through splits (Peyraguey, Rabaud, Doisy, Broustet and Nairac, Romer, Lamothe). Pexoto was absorbed into Rabaud in the 19th century.

graves_1959.title: Classification of Graves (1953, revised 1959)
graves_1959.note: A single unranked tier of Crus Classés, each listed for red, white or both. Laville Haut-Brion has been sold as La Mission Haut-Brion Blanc since 2009, and La Tour Haut-Brion stopped after the 2005 vintage.
graves_1959.revisions: First approved in August 1953, completed with additions in February 1959. Since 1987 all classified estates lie in the Pessac-Léognan appellation.

saint_emilion_2022.title: Classification of Saint-Émilion Grand Cru (2022)
saint_emilion_2022.note: Saint-Émilion is the only Bordeaux classification revised on a regular schedule. Estates are judged on tasting and other criteria, and the 2022 list has 85 estates. The three most famous former A estates chose to leave it.
saint_emilion_2022.approved: Approved by the INAO national committee on 8 September 2022; homologated by interministerial arrêté of 15 December 2022 (published 22 December 2022). Valid until the 2031 harvest.
saint_emilion_2022.withdrawals: Château Cheval Blanc and Château Ausone announced in July 2021 that they would not apply, criticising the weight of non-tasting criteria. Château Angélus withdrew on 5 January 2022. All three had been Premier Grand Cru Classé A in 2012, so they are no longer classified and only Figeac and Pavie hold the A rank.
saint_emilion_2022.history_2012: The 2012 list (announced 6 September 2012) had 82 estates: 18 Premiers Grands Crus Classés, 4 of them A (Ausone, Cheval Blanc, Angélus, Pavie), and 64 Grands Crus Classés. It followed the 2006 list annulled by the courts and faced lawsuits from demoted estates. The classification dates from 1955 and is meant to be revised every ten years.

crus_bourgeois.title: Classification des Crus Bourgeois du Médoc 2025
crus_bourgeois.note: Announced 12 February 2025 (at Wine Paris), replacing the 2020 list of 249. Revised every five years; counts refer to classified wines.

region.src: Agreste Nouvelle-Aquitaine (DRAAF), Essentiel no 80, June 2026: vines in production in Gironde

grape_share.basis: Share of vineyard area within each colour; red varieties 89% and white 11% of plantings

region.pomerol_note: Pomerol has no official classification of its wines.
region.left_right_bank: The Garonne and Dordogne rivers meet north of the city of Bordeaux to form the Gironde estuary. The Left Bank (Médoc and Graves) lies west of the Garonne and Gironde, and its reds are led by Cabernet Sauvignon. The Right Bank (Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and neighbours) lies around Libourne on the Dordogne, and its reds are led by Merlot with Cabernet Franc.

doubts: Official sites (crus-classes.com / grand-cru-classes-1855.com, bordeaux.com) could not be fetched in this session (permission not granted), so estate names follow the French Wikipedia list, iDealwine and estate articles rather than the Conseil des Grands Crus Classés.

Margaux and Cantenac merged in 2017 into the commune Margaux-Cantenac. 'commune' gives the historic village (Margaux or Cantenac) and 'current_commune' gives Margaux-Cantenac. The Margaux/Cantenac split (9 and 9, plus Labarde 2 and Arsac 1) follows French Wikipedia counts; Desmirail and Boyd-Cantenac placed in Cantenac (Decanter address for Desmirail), Rauzan-Gassies in Margaux though one French page lists it under Cantenac.
Cantemerle: English Wikipedia says added in 1856; French Wikipedia says a handwritten addition dated 16 September 1855.
Château Marquis d'Alesme: Wine Cellar Insider says 'Becker' was dropped around 2015; Wikipedia and iDealwine still use Marquis d'Alesme Becker.
Château Camensac vs Château de Camensac: both forms used; Pichon Baron full legal name is Château Pichon Longueville Baron.
Mouton Rothschild counted as Premier Cru (so Deuxièmes = 14).
Château La Mission Haut-Brion: Graves table says Pessac, estate article says Talence (used Talence).

Château Romer du Hayot: vineyard in Fargues per French Wikipedia list; its English article says commune Sauternes and the wine is now made in Barsac. Château de Myrat is in Barsac commune but listed with Sauternes appellation by sources.
Sauternes tiers: French Wikipedia list misgroups Rabaud-Promis, Sigalas Rabaud and Myrat; tiers taken from iDealwine and Wine Cellar Insider (11 Premiers, 15 Deuxièmes).

Saint-Émilion 2022: communes not given by INAO/AGCCSE, so commune is null; many estates lie outside Saint-Émilion commune (e.g. Saint-Christophe-des-Bardes, Saint-Étienne-de-Lisse). Spelling of names follows INAO with accents; AGCCSE uses upper case. One INAO web page list showed a duplicate La Couspaude and an extra 'La Dominique La Fleur Morange' entry, but the AGCCSE press kit and iDealwine give 71 unique names.
Arrêté date 15 December 2022 comes from English Wikipedia; Vitisphere says the decree was published 22 December 2022. Not checked on Légifrance.

Vineyard area: CIVB figure (110,000 ha, Key Facts 2021) is outdated after large-scale vine pulling; the 2025 figure (91,543 ha in production) is Agreste/DRAAF for Gironde, not CIVB. Grape shares are the latest CIVB figures found (2020 data) and are within-colour shares.
Cru Bourgeois 2025: Decanter says it applies from the 2025 vintage for five years; counts are of wines (170).
